revisions.body: Keep the focus on the contrast between appearance and examination: Charmides’ beauty and reputation are immediately available to view, whereas the temperance attributed to him cannot be established by appearance alone.
The setup names a specific task: Socrates is to examine whether Charmides has temperance. Its scope is this examination, not a broader program for the dialogue.

revisions.title: Critias’s report of Hesiod’s saying
revisions.body: Critias presents the saying as Hesiod’s and then develops its meaning for his own account; the passage does not stage Hesiod as entering the conversation.

body: "The scene that follows begins with a small deception. Critias summons Charmides on the pretext of a medical introduction, and suggests that Socrates pretend to know a headache remedy. Socrates accepts the ruse without hesitation. What makes the passage worth following closely is how he handles a cure invented as a lie: rather than dropping it once the boy arrives, he builds on it, layer by layer, until the pretend medicine has become a demand that Charmides submit his soul to treatment before his head. The fiction turns into the dialogue's real program."
